planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; as a true clumping bamboo it needs no rhizome barrier, but give it a wide open bed for its dense mature clump.

directions: Seabreeze bamboo forms thick-walled, closely spaced culms coated with a light powdery-blue bloom when new, topped with small, narrow dark green leaves that give the clump a fine, dense texture. Its sturdy, wind-flexing canes and unusual tolerance of salt spray make it one of the better bamboos for coastal windbreaks and hedges along the Gulf, where it holds up better than most bamboos to storm winds and salty air. As a true clumper it stays in a tight, slowly expanding footprint with no running rhizomes to contain, but young plants need protection the first couple of winters until established. Once rooted it grows quickly into a dense, screening thicket useful for property-line privacy or coastal windbreak plantings.

common_name: Baby Blue Bamboo (Barbellata Tropical Blue Bamboo)

planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a true clumper, it needs no containment barrier but appreciates a sheltered spot for its first winters.

directions: Barbellata is a smaller-statured selection of tropical blue bamboo, its upright canes dusted with the same soft, chalky-blue waxy bloom as the species but on a more garden-scaled clump reaching roughly 20-25 feet rather than the towering size of straight chungii. The tidy, tight clumping habit makes it a good choice for a large container specimen or a compact privacy screen where the full-size species would be too much bamboo for the space. It prefers fertile, evenly moist soil and full sun to part shade, and while young plants need frost protection, established clumps recover readily from occasional Gulf Coast cold snaps. Because it does not run by rhizome, it can be planted near patios, pools, or property lines without fear of it escaping into neighboring beds.

common_name: Stripestem Fernleaf Bamboo (Striped-Culm Dwarf Hedge Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this slow, compact clumper needs no rhizome barrier and works well in confined beds.

directions: This fine-textured hedge bamboo selection produces slender culms that emerge pink-tinged and fade through gold, marked with thin green stripes, above dense clusters of small, fern-like leaflets on starburst-like branchlets. It grows more slowly and stays more compact than many Bambusa multiplex forms, typically topping out near 10-12 feet, which makes it a manageable choice for a tight hedge or foundation screen rather than a large privacy wall. Being a genuine clumper, it never sends out running rhizomes and needs no containment barrier even in small Gulf Coast gardens. It tolerates the region's heat and humidity well once established and takes a light shearing to maintain a dense, uniform hedge line.

common_name: Asian Lemon Bamboo (Yellow-Striped Clumping Screen Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, well-mulched soil in full sun to dappled shade; being a true clumper it needs no rhizome barrier.

directions: Asian Lemon bamboo produces upright, lemon-yellow culms marked with irregular dark green stripes, with new growth flushing peach and pink before settling into its mature color, giving a vivid vertical accent among the clump. Its lower culm sheaths can be selectively pruned once canes have hardened off to display the colorful poles, while the branchy upper canopy still provides good screening density. As a tight clumping bamboo it stays where it is planted, making it a reasonable choice for a colorful accent screen or specimen grove close to structures. It performs best with consistent moisture and a generous mulch layer, and appreciates a sheltered site through its first Gulf Coast winters.

common_name: Asian Wonder Bamboo (Red-Sheathed Clumping Screen Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil with dappled shade and some morning or evening sun for best cane color; performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid.

directions: Asian Wonder is a distinctive clumping bamboo whose new canes emerge from ruby-red buds in vivid orange-red sheath color against dark, bloomy purple-green culms, aging to green as the clump matures and opening into a looser, more open form than many Fargesia. Its narrow, dark green leaves and colorful young growth make it a striking specimen or informal hedge for a partly shaded bed. Like other Fargesia, it forms a dense, non-running clump with no need for a rhizome barrier, but it shares the genus's dislike of prolonged, humid summer heat, so in zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens it does best with reliable afternoon shade and consistent moisture rather than full, baking sun. Winter cold hardiness is excellent, so the main limiting factor in the Deep South is summer heat stress rather than cold.

common_name: Green Screen Bamboo (Heat-Tolerant Robusta Clumping Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; this selection tolerates more sun and heat than typical Fargesia, making it a better fit for warmer zone 9 gardens.

directions: This vigorous robusta selection was chosen for exceptional vigor and forms a large, dense clump of stout canes topped with broad, glossy dark green leaves, quickly building an effective visual screen. Unlike many Fargesia, it tolerates considerably more direct sun and summer heat, which extends its usefulness a bit further south and into more open plantings than typical shade-loving umbrella or fountain bamboos. As a genuine clumper it forms a tight, expanding mass rather than running rhizomes, so it needs no containment barrier even in a small Gulf Coast lot. Give it fertile, evenly moist soil and room to reach its full 15-18 foot height for the best screening effect.

common_name: Jumbo Umbrella Bamboo (Tall Fast-Growing Clumping Hedge Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; its fast, upright growth makes it useful for building a tall hedge quickly.

directions: Jumbo is a larger-growing selection of umbrella bamboo, its canes emerging green and aging to yellow within a compact, tightly upright clump that reaches taller and fills in faster than the straight species. The dense, arching habit and fine foliage make it well suited to forming a quick living hedge or privacy screen along a fence line or property border. As with other Fargesia, it clumps tightly with no running rhizomes, so no barrier is needed, and it holds up to significant winter cold once established. In the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and steady soil moisture, since like its parent species it is less tolerant of prolonged summer heat than tropical clumping bamboos.

common_name: Black Stripe Bamboo (Megurochiku Striped-Groove Black Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this is a running bamboo.

directions: Megurochiku is an unusual form of black bamboo grown not for jet-black culms but for a bold black stripe that develops through the groove of each cane after a couple of seasons of sun exposure, set against olive-green rather than blackening culm color. New shoots emerge dark green in spring and the striping intensifies with age and light, giving a mature grove a distinctive striped-pole effect. Like all Phyllostachys it spreads by running rhizome and requires a physical barrier or regular trenching to stay contained in a Gulf Coast landscape. Once established it is drought tolerant and grows quickly into a dense, tall screen useful for privacy or as a specimen grove.

common_name: Kimmei Bamboo (Huangwenzhu Inversa Yellow-Culm Timber Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best culm color; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this is a fast-spreading running bamboo.

directions: This showy giant timber bamboo produces bright yellow culms marked with regular, even green stripes above each branch node, an inverse pattern of coloring compared to its sibling sport 'Aureocaulis' and one of the most vividly colored large bamboos in cultivation. Mature groves can reach impressive timber-bamboo scale with thick, strong canes, sizing up quickly once established in warm climates. As a running species it spreads aggressively by rhizome and absolutely requires a deep physical barrier or diligent trenching to prevent it from invading lawns and neighboring property. Given full sun and room to grow, it makes a dramatic large-scale screen or specimen grove, with new shoots edible when harvested young like other Phyllostachys.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil, including slightly alkaline sites, in full sun to partial shade; install a rhizome barrier before planting since this is a running bamboo.

directions: Yunzhu is a selection of the tough, adaptable species glauca that skips the bluish culm bloom typical of the species and instead develops distinctive dark spotting on its canes as they age, with spots gradually merging into larger blotches over time. It tolerates a wider range of soil conditions than many ornamental bamboos, including drier sites and slightly alkaline soil, and grows well in anything from full sun to partial shade. Being a running bamboo, it spreads by rhizome and needs a physical barrier or regular trenching to keep it from escaping into surrounding beds and lawn. Once established it is a durable, fast-growing choice for a tall screen or grove where soil conditions might challenge fussier bamboo species.

common_name: Cerise Charm Loropetalum (Kurobijin Deep-Purple Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage holds its deepest color with more direct sun.

directions: Cerise Charm is a compact Chinese fringe flower selection that holds season-long, deep reddish-purple foliage set off by bright cerise-pink, fringe-petaled spring flowers, with the strong color contrast making it a standout small accent shrub. Reaching only about 3-4 feet tall and wide after a decade, it stays far more compact than the species and most older purple-leaf cultivars, fitting easily into foundation plantings or small borders without frequent pruning. Like other Loropetalum, it tolerates the acidic soils common along the Gulf Coast and shrugs off short dry spells once established, though it flowers and colors best in full sun with only light afternoon shade in the hottest inland sites. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom flush to maintain its neat, rounded habit without sacrificing next year's flowers.
